title: How to diagnose thread deadlock: thread dump shows threads in BLOCKED state waiting for each other's locks: fix by consistent lock ordering, shorter critical sections, or using `tryLock` with timeout?
shortTitle: How do you diagnose a thread deadlock?

s1_definition.oneliner: A deadlock is threads holding each other's locks forever; find it in a thread dump's BLOCKED threads and fix it with consistent lock ordering or tryLock with a timeout.
s1_definition.profdef: A deadlock occurs when two or more threads each hold a lock the other needs and neither will ever release, so all of them wait forever. You diagnose it from a thread dump, where the deadlocked threads appear in the BLOCKED state, each "waiting to lock" a monitor that another thread "holds." Modern JVMs even print an explicit "Found one Java-level deadlock" section. You fix it with consistent global lock ordering, shorter critical sections, or lock acquisition with a timeout using `tryLock`.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A deadlock happens when two or more threads each hold a lock that another needs and none of them will release, so they all wait forever and make no progress. It needs four conditions at once – mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and a circular wait – and breaking any single one makes deadlock impossible. The most practical one to break is the circular wait. To diagnose a deadlock I take a thread dump with jstack or by sending the process a quit signal, and the deadlocked threads show up in the BLOCKED state, each one "waiting to lock" a monitor that another thread "holds." The HotSpot JVM is helpful here because it prints an explicit "Found one Java-level deadlock" section that names the threads and the locks, so I usually do not even have to trace the cycle by hand.

The fixes all come from breaking that circular wait. The cleanest is consistent lock ordering: I define a stable global order for locks, for example by account number, and always acquire them in that order so a cycle can never form. I also keep critical sections as short as possible and never call out to unknown code while holding a lock. When ordering is impractical, I use a ReentrantLock with tryLock and a timeout, so a thread that cannot get the second lock in time backs off, releases what it holds, and retries, which breaks the hold-and-wait condition. And for safety I add a runtime check using ThreadMXBean's findDeadlockedThreads, so if a deadlock ever forms in production it is detected, logged, and alerted instead of silently hanging.

In my banking work at National Bank of India, this was a real incident. Our transfer service hung with no errors and no CPU usage whenever two transfers ran at the same time in opposite directions, like Rajesh to Priya and Priya to Rajesh, because each thread locked its source account first and then blocked on the destination. The thread dump showed both threads BLOCKED in exactly that cycle. We fixed it by always locking the account with the lower account id first, which guarantees both transfers acquire the locks in the same order and the cycle can never happen. I also added the deadlock detector as a health check so we would catch any future ordering mistake immediately rather than discovering it from a frozen service.

Remember one sentence: How to diagnose thread deadlock: thread dump shows threads in BLOCKED state waiting for each other's locks: fix by consistent lock ordering, shorter critical sections, or using `tryLock` with timeout is fundamental knowledge for Java interviews and production banking work.
